chunks: "There are really three families. The first is single-point grounding, where every circuit gets its own wire or trace back to one common point.

That comes in a series or daisy-chain version, which is simple but lets circuits share return paths, and a parallel or star version, where each circuit has a dedicated return, so nothing shares an impedance except at the star point.

The second is multipoint grounding, which is basically a solid ground plane: every circuit drops straight into the plane through the nearest via, so the return path is as short and as low inductance as possible.

The third is a hybrid, where you use a plane for everything but partition the board so noisy digital and power returns stay in their own region and the sensitive analog area sits in a quiet corner, joined at one place.
Which one I pick depends on frequency. Below roughly a megahertz, the resistance of the ground path dominates and a star keeps return currents from sharing a drop.
Above ten megahertz or so, inductance dominates, long star traces become antennas and high-impedance paths, and you want a plane with lots of vias.
Most modern boards are a solid plane with careful placement, plus a star only at the board level, for example where a power input ties analog and digital returns together."
